title: Pan-Fried Black Pudding
subtitle: Sliced black pudding fried in a dry pan until the skin is crisp
excerpt: Black pudding cut into thick rounds and fried in a dry pan until the casing is crisp and the inside is hot and soft. The correct method for cooking black pudding as part of a full English or as a starter.
sourceNotes: Black pudding (blood sausage) has been made in Britain since at least the medieval period. Earliest British reference is in Cookery Manuscripts from the fourteenth century. Bury Black Pudding has been produced in Lancashire since at least 1810 and is the most famous British variety. Black pudding as part of the full English breakfast is documented from the Victorian era. Dorothy Hartley, Food in England (1954), black pudding documented as a regional speciality across northern England and Scotland.

content.text: Black pudding is a cooked blood sausage made from pig blood, fat, and oatmeal or barley. It is already cooked when you buy it and needs only to be sliced and heated through in a hot, dry pan until the casing is crisp and the inside is hot. The dry pan is important: black pudding has enough fat of its own. Adding oil makes it greasy; cooking it in a dry pan concentrates the flavour and crisps the skin.

items.prepNote: cut into rounds about 1.5 cm thick

content.text: Remove the outer casing from {{black-pudding}} of black pudding if it is inedible plastic; if it is natural casing, leave it on. Cut into rounds about 1.5 cm thick.
Heat a dry frying pan over medium-high heat. When the pan is hot, add the slices. Do not add any fat.
Cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side until the casing is well crisped and the rounds are hot through. The fat from the pudding will render into the pan as it heats.
Serve immediately as part of a full English breakfast, alongside fried eggs and toast, or as a starter with apple sauce and crusty bread.

rows.symptom: Black pudding falls apart in the pan
rows.cause: Sliced too thin or pan too hot
rows.fix: Cut rounds at least 1.5 cm thick. Very thin slices break up as the fat renders. Medium-high heat rather than full heat gives more control.

rows.symptom: Inside is still cold when the outside is crisp
rows.cause: Heat too high, crisped too fast
rows.fix: Reduce to medium heat. Once both sides are crisped, lower the heat and cover the pan for 1 minute to heat the inside through.
Use a dry pan. Black pudding renders its own fat as it cooks and does not need additional oil.
The pan must be properly hot before the black pudding goes in. A warm pan steams the casing; a hot one crisps it.

content.text: Black pudding has been made in Britain since the medieval period and remains a regional speciality in the north of England and Scotland. The most famous British variety is Bury Black Pudding from Lancashire, which has been made in the town since at least the early nineteenth century. Black pudding is one of the standard components of the full English breakfast, where it appears alongside bacon, eggs, sausages, baked beans, grilled tomatoes, and toast. In the north of England it also appears as a starter or snack, typically with apple sauce or on toast. Black pudding from Stornoway in the Outer Hebrides has its own distinct character from the Lancashire version.
